claims.claim: Current methods for recording muscle fiber activity via electromyography can resolve the activity of individual motor units in only a limited range of settings.
claims.source: However, our understanding of motor unit activity during natural behaviors is rudimentary due to the difficulty of recording spike trains from motor unit populations.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and comparison data showing limitations of traditional EMG methods.

claims.claim: Traditional EMG methods require that a subject's movements be highly restricted, typically in isometric force tasks, to prevent measurement artifacts.
claims.source: First, to prevent measurement artifacts, traditional EMG methods require that a subject's movements be highly restricted, typically in 'isometric' force tasks where subjects contract their muscles without moving their bodies (Bräcklein et al., 2022; Farina and Holobar, 2016; Marshall et al., 2022; Negro et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature describing limitations of traditional EMG.

claims.claim: Fine-wire electrodes typically cannot detect single motor unit activity in small muscles, including the muscles of mice or songbirds.
claims.source: Moreover, fine-wire electrodes typically cannot detect single motor unit activity in small muscles, including the muscles of widely used model systems such as mice or songbirds (Pearson et al., 2005; Srivastava et al., 2015; Pack et al., 2023), and surface electrode arrays are poorly tolerated by freely behaving animal subjects.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is contrasted with Myomatrix performance data.

claims.claim: Each motor neuron's action potential reliably evokes a single spike in its target muscle fibers.
claims.source: Because each action potential in a motor neuron reliably evokes a single spike in its target muscle fibers, action potentials recorded from muscle provide a high-resolution readout of motor neuron activity in the spinal cord and brainstem.
claims.evidence: This is established neuroscience knowledge about motor unit physiology.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays were fabricated using layers of polyimide and gold deposited on a carrier wafer.
claims.source: Layers of insulating polymer (polyimide) and conductive metal (gold) are successively deposited on a carrier wafer to form a flexible, 20- or 40-μm-thick electrode array of gold electrode contacts, which receive a surface treatment of PEDOT to improve recording properties (see 'Methods').
claims.evidence: This claim describes the fabrication process shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and detailed in Methods.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays have a thickness of 20 or 40 micrometers.
claims.source: The final device thickness was ~40 µm for the injectable (primate forelimb) design and ~20 µm for all other design variants.
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the Methods section.

claims.claim: Electrode contacts on Myomatrix arrays are coated with PEDOT:PSS to reduce electrode impedance.
claims.source: Electrode sites are then coated with a conductive polymer, PEDOT:PSS (Poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene)-poly(styrene-sulfonate)), (Cui and Martin, 2003; Dijk et al., 2020; Rossetti et al., 2019) to reduce the electrode impedance (Ludwig et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This fabrication detail is supported by citations to prior work on PEDOT:PSS properties.

claims.claim: PEDOT:PSS coating resulted in final electrode impedances of 5 kOhm or less for 100 × 200 μm electrode sites.
claims.source: PEDOT:PSS was deposited on the electrode contacts to a thickness of 100 nm using spin coating, resulting in final electrode impedances of 5 kOhm or less (100 × 200 um electrode sites).
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement of electrode impedance after PEDOT:PSS coating.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays can isolate individual motor units during mouse locomotion.
claims.source: Single motor units were routinely isolated during mouse locomotion in our Myomatrix recordings (Figure 1), but never in the fine-wire datasets from Miri et al., 2017 we reanalyzed or, to our knowledge, in any prior study.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and comparison with fine-wire EMG data.

claims.claim: Fine-wire EMG did not isolate any individual motor units during mouse locomotion in reanalyzed datasets from Miri et al., 2017.
claims.source: Single motor units were routinely isolated during mouse locomotion in our Myomatrix recordings (Figure 1), but never in the fine-wire datasets from Miri et al., 2017 we reanalyzed or, to our knowledge, in any prior study.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on reanalysis of published data using the same spike-sorting methods applied to Myomatrix data.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays have significantly higher signal-to-noise ratios than fine-wire EMG arrays in multiunit recordings.
claims.source: Moreover, in multiunit recordings, Myomatrix arrays have significantly higher signal-to-noise ratios than fine-wire EMG arrays (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3d.

claims.claim: SNR values from Myomatrix arrays are significantly greater than those from fine-wire EMG when all data are pooled (p=0.002).
claims.source: SNR values from Myomatrix arrays are significantly greater than those from fine-wire EMG, both when all data shown in (d) are pooled and when only data from day 14 are included (two-sample KS-test, p=0.002 and 0.038, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical test result comparing SNR measurements between Myomatrix and fine-wire EMG.

claims.claim: At least four Myomatrix threads bearing a total of 32 electrodes can be inserted into one mouse muscle.
claims.source: In contrast, at least four Myomatrix 'threads' (Figure 1a), bearing a total of 32 electrodes, can be inserted into one muscle (Figure 1c shows 5 of 32 channels recorded simultaneously from mouse triceps), greatly expanding the number of recording channels within a single muscle.
claims.evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claims.claim: Traditional fine-wire EMG typically provides only a single bipolar recording channel per mouse muscle.
claims.source: Second, because wire-based EMG requires inserting an additional wire for each additional electrode contact, only a single pair of wires (providing a single bipolar recording channel, Figure 1b, bottom) can be inserted into an individual mouse muscle in most cases (Miri et al., 2017; Tysseling et al., 2013; Tysseling et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim about limitations of fine-wire EMG is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays recorded isolated motor units for up to 4791 stride cycles in mice during continuous recording sessions lasting 10-60 minutes.
claims.source: In triceps recordings during locomotion in rodents (Figures 1 and 2c), isolated motor units were recorded for up to 4791 stride cycles (mice) or 491 stride cycles (rats) during continuous recording sessions lasting 10–60 min.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of recording stability during behavior.

claims.claim: Individual motor units were most frequently recorded in the first 2 weeks of chronic recordings.
claims.source: Although individual motor units were most frequently recorded in the first 2 wk of chronic recordings (see main text), Myomatrix arrays also isolate individual motor units after much longer periods of chronic implantation, as shown here where spikes from two individual motor units (colored boxes in bottom trace) were isolated during locomotion 65 d after implantation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3e and discussed in the main text.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays isolated individual motor units during locomotion 65 days after implantation.
claims.source: Although individual motor units were most frequently recorded in the first 2 wk of chronic recordings (see main text), Myomatrix arrays also isolate individual motor units after much longer periods of chronic implantation, as shown here where spikes from two individual motor units (colored boxes in bottom trace) were isolated during locomotion 65 d after implantation.
claims.evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the example recording shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3e.

claims.claim: Myomatrix recordings in nonhuman primates maintained single-unit isolation across 1292 reaching trials collected over 97 minutes.
claims.source: Myomatrix recordings in behaving nonhuman primates were similarly long-lived, as in the dataset shown in Figure 3, where single-unit isolation was maintained across 1292 reaching trials collected over 97 min.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of recording stability in primates shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The duration of single-unit EMG recording was limited by the willingness of the animal to continue performing the behavior, rather than a loss of signal isolation.
claims.source: In each of these datasets, the duration of single-unit EMG recording was limited by the willingness of the animal to continue performing the behavior, rather than a loss of signal isolation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that recordings remained stable until behavioral sessions ended.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays did not show voltage artifacts at any point in the stride cycle during rodent locomotion recordings.
claims.source: In recordings from rodents during locomotion (Figures 1b and 2c), we did not observe voltage artifacts at any point in the stride cycle (e.g. when the paw of the recorded limb first touches the ground in each stride cycle; Figure 2c, black arrowhead).
claims.evidence: This observation is based on examination of the recorded data during locomotion.

claims.claim: Movement artifacts were absent during active arm movements in monkeys with peak fingertip speeds of approximately 15 cm/s and peak elbow angle velocity of approximately 40°/s.
claims.source: Movement artifacts were similarly absent during active arm movements in monkeys (peak fingertip speeds ~15 cm/s; peak elbow angle velocity ~40°/s, Figure 3b and e), during passive jaw displacement in anesthetized mice (Figure 2b), or in the other anesthetized preparations shown in Figure 2.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of recordings during movements with measured kinematics.

claims.claim: Injectable Myomatrix arrays yielded motor unit recordings during arm movements in rhesus macaques.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3a–d, injectable Myomatrix arrays yielded motor unit recordings during arm movements.
claims.evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Thirteen motor units were recorded simultaneously during a single trial in which a monkey reached to a target.
claims.source: Tick marks in Figure 3d show the activity of 13 motor units recorded simultaneously during a single trial in which a monkey was cued (by a force perturbation which causes an extension of the elbow joint) to reach to a target.
claims.evidence: This is a direct count of motor units isolated from the data shown in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: Conventional fine-wire EMG inserted into the same muscle as Myomatrix arrays yielded only a single trace reflecting the activity of an unknown number of motor units.
claims.source: In contrast to the ensemble of motor units recorded with a Myomatrix probe, conventional fine-wire EMGs inserted into the same muscle (in a separate recording session) yielded only a single trace reflecting the activity of an unknown number of motor units (Figure 3e, middle).
claims.evidence: This comparison is based on data from the same muscle in the same animal but different recording sessions.

claims.claim: Polyimide was selected as a substrate material due to its strength and flexibility and the ease with which sub-millimeter features could be defined.
claims.source: We selected polyimide as a substrate material due to its strength and flexibility and the ease with which we could define electrode contacts, suture holes, and other sub-millimeter features that facilitate implantation and recording stability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–e).
claims.evidence: This is a design rationale based on material properties.

claims.claim: The fabrication pipeline allows rapid development and refinement of multiple array designs.
claims.source: This fabrication pipeline allows the rapid development and refinement of multiple array designs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–g).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the variety of designs shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays can record from forelimb, hindlimb, orofacial, pelvic, vocal, and respiratory muscles.
claims.source: Below, we show how Myomatrix arrays provide high-resolution measurements of motor unit activation in a variety of species and muscle groups including forelimb, hindlimb, orofacial, pelvic, vocal, and respiratory muscles.
claims.evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Myomatrix recordings isolated motor units from the mouse triceps during a head-fixed pellet reaching task.
claims.source: Beyond the locomotor and postural signals shown in Figure 1, Myomatrix recordings from mouse triceps also provided single-unit EMG data during a head-fixed reaching task (Figure 2a).
claims.evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays recorded single motor unit EMG data from the mouse superficial masseter muscle during reflexive muscle contraction evoked by passive jaw displacement.
claims.source: Figure 2b shows single motor unit EMG data recorded from the superficial masseter (jaw) muscle when reflexive muscle contraction was obtained by passively displacing the jaw of an anesthetized mouse.
claims.evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays obtained isolated motor units from rat triceps during locomotion.
claims.source: To extend these methods across species, we collected Myomatrix recordings from muscles of the rat forelimb, obtaining isolated motor units from the triceps during locomotion (Figure 2c) and a digit-flexing muscle in the lower forearm during head-free reaching (Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays can isolate motor unit waveforms evoked by direct optogenetic stimulation of spinal motor neurons.
claims.source: Myomatrix arrays can furthermore isolate motor unit waveforms evoked by direct optogenetic stimulation of spinal motor neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2e.

claims.claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the spinal cord evokes spiking in single motor units with millisecond-scale timing jitter.
claims.source: Figure 2e shows recordings of light-evoked spikes in the mouse bulbospongiosus muscle (BSM, a pelvic muscle that wraps around the base of the penis in male mice), demonstrating that optogenetic stimulation of the spinal cord evokes spiking in single motor units with millisecond-scale timing jitter (Figure 2e, center) and with latencies (Figure 2e, right) consistent with the latencies of recordings obtained with fine-wire electrodes (Lenschow et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of optogenetically evoked responses shown in Figure 2e.

claims.claim: Optogenetically evoked motor unit spikes have latencies between 10 and 15 ms, consistent with results obtained from traditional fine-wire electrodes in mice.
claims.source: Figure 2e shows recordings of light-evoked spikes in the mouse bulbospongiosus muscle (BSM, a pelvic muscle that wraps around the base of the penis in male mice), demonstrating that optogenetic stimulation of the spinal cord evokes spiking in single motor units with millisecond-scale timing jitter (Figure 2e, center) and with latencies (Figure 2e, right) consistent with the latencies of recordings obtained with fine-wire electrodes (Lenschow et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim compares Myomatrix measurements with prior fine-wire EMG results.

claims.claim: Simple modifications of the basic electrode array design allowed high-resolution recordings from hindlimb muscles in cats.
claims.source: Beyond rodents, simple modifications of the basic electrode array design (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f) allowed us to obtain high-resolution recordings from hindlimb muscles in cats (Figure 2f), vocal and respiratory muscles in songbirds (Figure 2g and h, see also Zia et al., 2020), body wall muscles in moth larvae (Figure 2i), and leg muscles in frogs (Figure 2j).
claims.evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2f.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays obtained high-resolution recordings from vocal and respiratory muscles in songbirds.
claims.source: Beyond rodents, simple modifications of the basic electrode array design (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f) allowed us to obtain high-resolution recordings from hindlimb muscles in cats (Figure 2f), vocal and respiratory muscles in songbirds (Figure 2g and h, see also Zia et al., 2020), body wall muscles in moth larvae (Figure 2i), and leg muscles in frogs (Figure 2j).
claims.evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2g and h.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays obtained high-resolution recordings from body wall muscles in moth larvae.
claims.source: Beyond rodents, simple modifications of the basic electrode array design (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f) allowed us to obtain high-resolution recordings from hindlimb muscles in cats (Figure 2f), vocal and respiratory muscles in songbirds (Figure 2g and h, see also Zia et al., 2020), body wall muscles in moth larvae (Figure 2i), and leg muscles in frogs (Figure 2j).
claims.evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2i.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays obtained high-resolution recordings from leg muscles in frogs.
claims.source: Beyond rodents, simple modifications of the basic electrode array design (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f) allowed us to obtain high-resolution recordings from hindlimb muscles in cats (Figure 2f), vocal and respiratory muscles in songbirds (Figure 2g and h, see also Zia et al., 2020), body wall muscles in moth larvae (Figure 2i), and leg muscles in frogs (Figure 2j).
claims.evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2j.

claims.claim: The mouse lateral head of the triceps muscle is approximately 9 mm in length with a mass of 0.02 g.
claims.source: These methods allow the user to record simultaneously from ensembles of single motor units (Figure 1c and d) in freely behaving animals, even from small muscles including the lateral head of the triceps muscle in mice (approximately 9 mm in length with a mass of 0.02 g; Mathewson et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This anatomical measurement is cited from prior literature.

claims.claim: In songbird vocal muscles, most individual motor neurons innervate only 1-3 muscle fibers.
claims.source: These approaches will be particularly valuable in muscles in which each motor neuron controls a very small number of muscle fibers, allowing fine control of oculomotor muscles in mammals as well as vocal muscles in songbirds (Figure 2g), in which most individual motor neurons innervate only 1–3 muscle fibers (Adam et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This anatomical fact about songbird vocal muscles is cited from prior literature.

claims.claim: Motor unit action potential waveforms from individual motor units were identified using analysis methods previously used to sort spikes from neural data.
claims.source: Motor unit action potential waveforms from individual motor units were identified with analysis methods previously used to sort spikes from neural data.
claims.evidence: This describes the analytical approach used to process Myomatrix data.

claims.claim: Myomatrix signals were band-passed between 350 and 7000 Hz.
claims.source: In all cases, Myomatrix signals (sampling rate 30 or 40 kHz) were first band-passed between 350 and 7000 Hz.
claims.evidence: This is a data processing parameter used in the analysis.

claims.claim: Kilosort version 2.5 was adapted to sort waveforms into clusters arising from individual motor units.
claims.source: We therefore adapted Kilosort version 2.5 (Pachitariu et al., 2023; Steinmetz et al., 2021) and wrote custom MATLAB and Python code to sort waveforms into clusters arising from individual motor units (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e–h).
claims.evidence: This describes the spike-sorting software and modifications used for analysis.

claims.claim: The spike-sorting code including modifications to Kilosort is available at https://github.com/JonathanAMichaels/PixelProcessingPipeline/releases/tag/v0.9.
claims.source: Our spike-sorting code, which includes the above-mentioned modifications to Kilosort, is available at https://github.com/JonathanAMichaels/PixelProcessingPipeline/releases/tag/v0.9 (copy archived at Michaels, 2023).
claims.evidence: This provides the location of the code repository for reproducibility.

claims.claim: The close electrode spacing and proximity of contacts to muscle fibers in Myomatrix arrays ensure that each channel records from a much smaller volume of tissue than skin-surface arrays.
claims.source: In Myomatrix arrays, the close electrode spacing and very close proximity of the contacts to muscle fibers ensure that each Myomatrix channel records from a much smaller volume of tissue than skin-surface arrays.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the physical design of the arrays.

claims.claim: Myomatrix recordings include a smaller number of motor units represented on each recording channel compared to skin-surface recordings.
claims.source: This difference in recording volume in turn creates different challenges for motor unit isolation: compared to skin-surface recordings, Myomatrix recordings include a smaller number of motor units represented on each recording channel, with individual motor units appearing on a smaller fraction of the sensors than typical in a skin-surface recording.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of the recording geometry.

claims.claim: Skin-surface EMG analysis methods typically use source-separation approaches that assume each sensor receives input from most or all of the individual sources within the muscle.
claims.source: Specifically, skin-surface EMG analysis methods typically use source-separation approaches that assume that each sensor receives input from most or all of the individual sources within the muscle as is presumably the case in the data.
claims.evidence: This describes the analytical assumptions underlying skin-surface EMG analysis.

claims.claim: The much sparser recordings from Myomatrix are better decomposed using methods like Kilosort, which are designed to extract waveforms that appear only on a small, spatially restricted subset of recording channels.
claims.source: In contrast, the much sparser recordings from Myomatrix are better decomposed using methods like Kilosort, which are designed to extract waveforms that appear only on a small, spatially restricted subset of recording channels.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological inference about the appropriate analysis approach for Myomatrix data.

claims.claim: In over 100 Myomatrix injections performed in rhesus macaques, there were zero cases in which arrays broke such that electrode material was left behind in the recorded muscle.
claims.source: Moreover, in over 100 Myomatrix injections performed in rhesus macaques, there were zero cases in which Myomatrix arrays broke such that electrode material was left behind in the recorded muscle, representing a substantial improvement over traditional fine-wire approaches, in which breakage of the bent wire tip regularly occurs (Loeb and Gans, 1986).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative safety measurement from the primate experiments.

claims.claim: Breakage of the bent wire tip regularly occurs with traditional fine-wire EMG approaches.
claims.source: Moreover, in over 100 Myomatrix injections performed in rhesus macaques, there were zero cases in which Myomatrix arrays broke such that electrode material was left behind in the recorded muscle, representing a substantial improvement over traditional fine-wire approaches, in which breakage of the bent wire tip regularly occurs (Loeb and Gans, 1986).
claims.evidence: This is a known limitation of fine-wire EMG cited from prior literature.

claims.claim: Insertion and removal of injectable Myomatrix devices appeared to be comparable or superior to traditional fine-wire EMG electrodes in terms of ease of injection, ease of removal, and animal comfort.
claims.source: Insertion and removal of injectable Myomatrix devices appeared to be comparable or superior to traditional fine-wire EMG electrodes (in which a 'hook' is formed by bending back the uninsulated tip of the recording wire) in terms of ease of injection, ease of removal of both the cannula and the array itself, and animal comfort.
claims.evidence: This is a qualitative assessment based on experimental experience.

claims.claim: The songbird dataset shown in Figure 2g includes single-unit data from 8101 respiratory cycles collected over 74 minutes.
claims.source: For example, the songbird dataset shown in Figure 2g includes single-unit data from 8101 respiratory cycles collected over 74 min, and, like the other acute recordings shown in Figure 2, recordings were ended by the experimenter rather than because of a loss of signal from individual motor units.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of recording duration in songbirds.

claims.claim: Applying Myomatrix technology to human motor unit recordings will create novel opportunities to diagnose motor pathologies and quantify the effects of therapeutic interventions.
claims.source: Applying Myomatrix technology to human motor unit recordings, particularly by using the minimally invasive injectable designs shown in Figure 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1g and i, will create novel opportunities to diagnose motor pathologies and quantify the effects of therapeutic interventions in restoring motor function.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future applications.

claims.claim: Myomatrix arrays might significantly reduce the risk and discomfort of clinical EMG procedures while also greatly increasing the accuracy with which human motor function can be quantified.
claims.source: Moreover, because Myomatrix arrays are far more flexible than the rigid needles commonly used to record clinical EMG, our technology might significantly reduce the risk and discomfort of such procedures while also greatly increasing the accuracy with which human motor function can be quantified.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential clinical benefits based on material properties.

claims.claim: The nervous system's control of skeletal motor output is ultimately mediated by motor units.
claims.source: The nervous system's control of skeletal motor output is ultimately mediated by 'motor units,' each of which consists of a single motor neuron and the muscle fibers it activates, producing motor unit action potentials (Figure 1a) that generate muscle force to produce movement (Manuel et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established neuroscience knowledge about motor control.

claims.claim: A motor unit consists of a single motor neuron and the muscle fibers it activates.
claims.source: The nervous system's control of skeletal motor output is ultimately mediated by 'motor units,' each of which consists of a single motor neuron and the muscle fibers it activates, producing motor unit action potentials (Figure 1a) that generate muscle force to produce movement (Manuel et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is the standard definition of a motor unit in neuroscience.

claims.claim: Recent decades have seen tremendous advances in understanding the physiological mechanisms by which the brain controls complex motor behaviors.
claims.source: Recent decades have seen tremendous advances in our understanding of the physiological mechanisms by which the brain controls complex motor behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by subsequent citations.

claims.claim: Tools to record neural activity at scale have been critical to advances in understanding motor control.
claims.source: Critical to these advances have been tools to record neural activity at scale (Steinmetz et al., 2018; Urai et al., 2022), which, when combined with novel algorithms for behavioral tracking (Machado et al., 2015; Berman et al., 2014; Pereira et al., 2019; Mathis et al., 2020; Wiltschko et al., 2020), can reveal how neural activity shapes behavior (Hernández et al., 2022; Vyas et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Current methods for observing the nervous system's motor output lag far behind neural recording technologies.
claims.source: In contrast, current methods for observing the nervous system's motor output lag far behind neural recording technologies.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative assessment of the state of the field that motivates the work.

claims.claim: Traditional methods for recording muscle fiber activity via electromyography include fine wires inserted into muscles and electrode arrays placed on the surface of the skin.
claims.source: Traditional methods for recording muscle fiber activity via electromyography (EMG) include fine wires inserted into muscles and electrode arrays placed on the surface of the skin (Loeb and Gans, 1986).
claims.evidence: This describes standard EMG methods cited from prior literature.

claims.claim: Surface electrode arrays are poorly tolerated by freely behaving animal subjects.
claims.source: Moreover, fine-wire electrodes typically cannot detect single motor unit activity in small muscles, including the muscles of widely used model systems such as mice or songbirds (Pearson et al., 2005; Srivastava et al., 2015; Pack et al., 2023), and surface electrode arrays are poorly tolerated by freely behaving animal subjects.
claims.evidence: This is a practical limitation of surface arrays based on experimental experience.

claims.claim: High-resolution motor unit recordings have previously been achieved by directly recording from motor neuron cell bodies in vertebrates.
claims.source: Although this resolution has previously been achieved in moving subjects by directly recording from motor neuron cell bodies in vertebrates (Hoffer et al., 1981; Robinson, 1970; Hyngstrom et al., 2007) and using fine-wire electrodes in moving insects (Pflüger and Burrows, 1978; Putney et al., 2023), both methods are extremely challenging and can only target a small subset of species and motor unit populations.
claims.evidence: This claim about prior methods is supported by citations to earlier work.

claims.claim: Fine-wire electrodes have been used to achieve high-resolution motor unit recordings in moving insects.
claims.source: Although this resolution has previously been achieved in moving subjects by directly recording from motor neuron cell bodies in vertebrates (Hoffer et al., 1981; Robinson, 1970; Hyngstrom et al., 2007) and using fine-wire electrodes in moving insects (Pflüger and Burrows, 1978; Putney et al., 2023), both methods are extremely challenging and can only target a small subset of species and motor unit populations.
claims.evidence: This claim about prior methods is supported by citations to earlier work.

claims.claim: Direct recording from motor neurons and fine-wire electrodes in insects are extremely challenging methods that can only target a small subset of species and motor unit populations.
claims.source: Although this resolution has previously been achieved in moving subjects by directly recording from motor neuron cell bodies in vertebrates (Hoffer et al., 1981; Robinson, 1970; Hyngstrom et al., 2007) and using fine-wire electrodes in moving insects (Pflüger and Burrows, 1978; Putney et al., 2023), both methods are extremely challenging and can only target a small subset of species and motor unit populations.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of prior methods.

claims.claim: Combining high-resolution EMG with precise measurement of muscle length and force output will help untangle the complex relationship between neural control, body kinematics, and muscle force.
claims.source: Of further interest will be combining high-resolution EMG with precise measurement of muscle length and force output to untangle the complex relationship between neural control, body kinematics, and muscle force that characterizes dynamic motor behavior.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about future research directions.

claims.claim: Combining Myomatrix recordings with high-density brain recordings or targeted manipulations of neural activity can reveal how central circuits shape motor activity.
claims.source: Similarly, combining Myomatrix recordings with high-density brain recordings or targeted manipulations of neural activity can reveal how central circuits shape and reshape motor activity and – in contrast to the multiunit signals typically obtained from traditional EMG in animals – reveal how neural dynamics in cortical, subcortical, and spinal circuits shape the spiking patterns of individual motor neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future applications.

claims.claim: The expansion of access to high-resolution EMG signals across muscle groups, species, and behaviors is the chief impact of the Myomatrix project.
claims.source: This expansion of access to high-resolution EMG signals – across muscle groups, species, and behaviors – is the chief impact of the Myomatrix project.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the work.

claims.claim: The microfabrication process consists of depositing and patterning a series of polymer and metal layers using spin coating, photolithography, etching, and evaporation processes.
claims.source: The microfabrication process (schematized in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) consists of depositing and patterning a series of polymer (polyimide) and metal (gold) layers using a combination of spin coating, photolithography, etching, and evaporation processes, as described previously (Zia et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2022; Zia et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes the fabrication methods with citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The fabrication methods allow very fine pitch escape routing with less than 10 μm spacing between traces.
claims.source: These methods allow very fine pitch escape routing (<10 µm spacing between the thin 'escape' traces connecting electrode contacts to the connector), spatial alignment between the multiple layers of polyimide and gold that constitute each device, and precise definition of 'via' pathways that connect different layers of the device.
claims.evidence: This describes a technical capability of the fabrication process.

claims.claim: Gold EMG recording electrode sites are formed by removing the top polyimide layer over each electrode site using reactive ion etching with O2 and SF6 plasma at a 5:1 ratio.
claims.source: Once all the metal and polyimide layers have been deposited and patterned on carrier wafers, the gold EMG recording electrode sites are formed by removing the top polyimide layer over each electrode site using reactive ion etching process (O2 and SF6 plasma, 5:1 ratio).
claims.evidence: This is a specific fabrication parameter.

claims.claim: PEDOT:PSS was deposited on the electrode contacts to a thickness of 100 nm using spin coating.
claims.source: PEDOT:PSS was deposited on the electrode contacts to a thickness of 100 nm using spin coating, resulting in final electrode impedances of 5 kOhm or less (100 × 200 um electrode sites).
claims.evidence: This is a specific fabrication parameter.

claims.claim: An Optec Femtosecond laser system was used to cut the electrode arrays into the desired shape/pattern.
claims.source: Once all layers have been deposited on the carrier wafer, the wafer is transferred to an Optec Femtosecond laser system, which is used to cut the electrode arrays into the shape/pattern needed based on the target muscle group and animal species.
claims.evidence: This describes a fabrication step.

claims.claim: A Lambda flip-chip bonder was used to bond high-density connectors to the surface of the electrode array.
claims.source: The final fabrication step is bonding a high-density connector (Omnetics, Inc) to the surface of the electrode array using a Lambda flip-chip bonder (Finetech, Inc).

claims.claim: For chronic EMG recording in mice and rats, the array's connector was secured to the skull using dental cement.

results.result: Myomatrix arrays are flexible, high-density electrode devices fabricated from polyimide and gold layers with PEDOT:PSS coating, achieving 20-40 μm thickness and electrode impedances ≤5 kΩ. The fabrication pipeline enables rapid design iteration for different muscle groups and species.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 and C69-C74 provide detailed fabrication specifications with specific measurements (thickness, impedance, layer composition). The material selection rationale (C27) and design flexibility (C28) are demonstrated by multiple array variants shown in figures. The technical specifications are internally consistent and well-documented.

results.result: Myomatrix arrays successfully isolate individual motor units during mouse locomotion, a capability not achieved by fine-wire EMG in the same behavioral context. Myomatrix arrays provide 32 electrodes per muscle versus a single bipolar channel for fine-wire EMG, with significantly higher SNR (p=0.002).
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 are supported by direct comparison using identical spike-sorting methods on both datasets (Figure 1). The statistical comparison (C14) uses appropriate tests (KS-test) with significant p-values. The channel count advantage (C15-C16) is demonstrated experimentally and represents a fundamental hardware difference.

results.result: Myomatrix arrays provide stable motor unit recordings over extended periods: up to 4791 stride cycles (10-60 min) in mice, 1292 trials (97 min) in primates, and 8101 respiratory cycles (74 min) in songbirds. Individual units can be recorded up to 65 days post-implantation, though yield is highest in the first 2 weeks.
results.evaluation: Claims C17, C20, and C53 provide specific quantitative measurements of recording duration across species. The chronic recording capability (C18-C19) is demonstrated with example data at 65 days. Claim C21 about behavioral limitation is a reasonable inference but cannot be definitively proven without attempting longer sessions.

results.result: Myomatrix arrays show minimal movement artifacts during active behaviors, including rodent locomotion and primate reaching movements with peak speeds of ~15 cm/s and elbow velocities of ~40°/s.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C23 are supported by visual inspection of recorded traces during movement (Figures 1b, 2c, 3b). The absence of artifacts at specific gait events (paw contact) and during measured movement velocities provides quantitative support. However, the assessment relies on qualitative observation rather than systematic artifact quantification.

results.result: Injectable Myomatrix arrays successfully recorded 13 motor units simultaneously during primate reaching, compared to only multiunit signals from fine-wire EMG in the same muscle. Zero electrode breakages occurred in >100 primate injections, compared to regular breakage with fine-wire approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 demonstrate superior performance in primates with direct within-animal comparison (though in separate sessions). The safety data (C50) provides a large sample size (n>100) with zero failures. However, C52's claim of "comparable or superior" ease and comfort is qualitative and lacks systematic measurement.

results.result: Myomatrix arrays successfully recorded motor unit activity across diverse muscle groups (forelimb, hindlimb, orofacial, pelvic, vocal, respiratory) and species (mice, rats, cats, songbirds, frogs, moth larvae), including during optogenetic stimulation with latencies consistent with prior fine-wire measurements.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C39 are each supported by specific experimental demonstrations in Figure 2. The optogenetic validation (C34-C35) provides independent confirmation of recording accuracy by comparing latencies to published fine-wire data. The breadth of applications demonstrates versatility, though sample sizes per condition are not specified.

results.result: Motor units were identified using adapted spike-sorting algorithms (Kilosort 2.5 and PCA-based methods) with specific quality criteria: <1% ISI violations, absolute refractory period <1 ms, and waveform consistency. The analysis approach differs from skin-surface EMG methods due to sparser spatial sampling in Myomatrix recordings.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 describe established methods with appropriate citations and code availability (C45). The quality control criteria (C81-C83) are standard in the field. The methodological rationale (C46-C49) correctly identifies differences in recording geometry that necessitate different analysis approaches. However, no systematic validation of sorting accuracy is provided.

results.result: Surgical implantation procedures and data acquisition methods are described, including chronic skull mounting, intramuscular threading with barb-based anchoring, and flexible recording configurations (32 unipolar or 16 bipolar channels at 30-40 kHz sampling).
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C85 provide detailed methodological descriptions that are internally consistent and supported by schematic figures. The procedures are standard surgical techniques adapted for the specific hardware. These are primarily methodological details rather than novel findings.

results.result: Traditional EMG methods (fine-wire and surface electrodes) have significant limitations: requirement for restricted movements to avoid artifacts, inability to detect single units in small muscles, poor tolerance by freely behaving animals, and extreme technical difficulty of alternative approaches like direct motor neuron recording.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 and C60-C65 accurately characterize limitations of existing methods based on appropriate citations and are consistent with field knowledge. These claims establish the motivation for the work. However, they represent assessment of prior work rather than new findings.

results.result: Background claims about motor unit physiology and the state of motor control research: motor units consist of a motor neuron and its innervated muscle fibers, each action potential reliably evokes muscle fiber spikes, and neural recording technologies have advanced significantly.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C56-C59 represent established neuroscience knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. These are accurate background statements that contextualize the work but do not constitute novel findings.

results.result: Anatomical facts cited from literature: mouse triceps lateral head is ~9 mm long with 0.02 g mass, and songbird vocal motor neurons innervate only 1-3 muscle fibers.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 are factual statements appropriately cited from prior literature (Mathewson et al., 2012; Adam et al., 2021). These provide context for the technical achievement but are not original findings of this work.

results.result: Speculative claims about future applications: Myomatrix technology could enable clinical diagnosis of motor pathologies, reduce risk/discomfort of EMG procedures, and reveal how neural circuits shape motor output when combined with brain recordings.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 and C66-C67 are explicitly speculative ("will create," "might significantly reduce," "will be") about potential future applications. While plausible based on the demonstrated capabilities, these represent hypotheses about future work rather than supported findings from the current study.

results.result: The chief impact of the Myomatrix project is expanding access to high-resolution EMG signals across muscle groups, species, and behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 is a summary statement about significance that is well-supported by the breadth of demonstrations across species (C2, C29-C39), muscle groups, and behavioral contexts. This represents a reasonable assessment of the work's contribution based on the presented evidence.

results.result: All animal procedures received appropriate institutional and regulatory approvals from multiple institutions (Emory University, Champalimaud Centre, and others).
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 provide specific protocol numbers and regulatory approvals. These are verifiable administrative facts required for publication. While important for ethical compliance, these are not scientific findings.

results.result: Myomatrix arrays are a novel class of high-density, flexible electrode devices that enable stable recordings from individual motor units during natural behaviors across multiple species including mice, rats, primates, songbirds, frogs, and insects.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. The editor states this is an 'important paper' reporting 'major technical advances for in vivo intramuscular electrical recording from multiple motor units in behaving animals' with 'compelling demonstrations of the efficacy of this new technique in multiple animal species.' Reviewers note 'the main significance of this manuscript is the application of this new technology to different muscles and animal species during naturalistic behaviors' and praise 'convincing examples of EMG recordings with high signal quality using this new technology from a wide array of animal species, muscles, and behavior.'

results.result: Traditional EMG methods have significant limitations: they require restricted movements (typically isometric tasks), fine-wire electrodes cannot detect single motor units in small muscles like those of mice or songbirds, and current methods for observing motor output lag behind neural recording technologies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these motivating claims about the limitations of existing methods without challenge. One reviewer explicitly states that 'neurophysiology faces an urgent need for methods to record their activity at high resolution and scale in intact animals during natural movement' and that 'current methods of recording EMG using intramuscular fine-wire electrodes do not allow for isolation of motor units and are limited by the muscle size and the type of behavior.' These claims provide accepted context for the significance of the new technology.

results.result: Myomatrix arrays routinely isolated individual motor units during mouse locomotion, whereas fine-wire EMG from reanalyzed datasets (Miri et al., 2017) never isolated individual motor units. Myomatrix arrays also showed significantly higher signal-to-noise ratios than fine-wire EMG (p=0.002 when all data pooled).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the superior performance of Myomatrix over traditional methods. One reviewer states 'the claims are justified by the data' and another notes 'convincing examples of EMG recordings with high signal quality.' The direct comparison with fine-wire EMG and statistical evidence of superior SNR is accepted without critique, supporting the claim that Myomatrix represents a substantial technical advance over existing methods.

results.result: At least four Myomatrix threads bearing 32 electrodes total can be inserted into one mouse muscle, greatly expanding recording channels compared to traditional fine-wire EMG which typically provides only a single bipolar channel per mouse muscle.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this claim as part of the demonstrated technical advantages. One reviewer specifically highlights 'the design included suture holes and pull-on tabs that facilitate implantation and ensure stable recordings over months' as a strength. The multi-channel capability is implicitly endorsed through reviewers' acceptance of the multi-unit recordings shown throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Myomatrix arrays maintained stable single-unit recordings over extended periods: up to 4791 stride cycles in mice (10-60 min sessions), 1292 reaching trials in primates (97 min), and individual motor units were recorded up to 65 days post-implantation, with recording duration limited by animal behavior rather than signal loss.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm recording stability as a key strength. One reviewer notes 'the design included suture holes and pull-on tabs that facilitate implantation and ensure stable recordings over months.' The editor emphasizes 'compelling demonstrations of the efficacy of this new technique' and reviewers state 'the claims are justified by the data,' accepting the long-term stability claims without requesting additional validation.

results.result: Myomatrix arrays showed no voltage artifacts during movement, including at stride cycle contact points in rodent locomotion and during active arm movements in monkeys with peak speeds of ~15 cm/s and elbow velocities of ~40°/s.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the absence of movement artifacts as demonstrated. One reviewer notes that 'methods are explained clearly, and the claims are justified by the data.' The lack of artifacts during naturalistic behaviors is implicitly endorsed through reviewers' acceptance that the technology enables recordings 'during natural movement' and 'naturalistic behaviors' without raising concerns about artifact contamination.

results.result: Injectable Myomatrix arrays recorded 13 motor units simultaneously during reaching in rhesus macaques, whereas conventional fine-wire EMG in the same muscle yielded only a single trace reflecting an unknown number of motor units.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the primate recordings as part of the compelling multi-species demonstration. The editor notes 'compelling demonstrations of the efficacy of this new technique in multiple animal species' and reviewers state they 'presented convincing examples of EMG recordings with high signal quality using this new technology from a wide array of animal species.' The direct comparison with fine-wire EMG in primates is accepted without challenge.

results.result: Myomatrix arrays successfully recorded from diverse muscle groups and species including mouse triceps (reaching, locomotion), masseter (jaw), rat triceps and digit flexors, optogenetically-evoked responses in mouse pelvic muscle, and muscles in cats, songbirds, moth larvae, and frogs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly endorse the breadth of applications as a key contribution. One reviewer states 'they presented convincing examples of EMG recordings with high signal quality using this new technology from a wide array of animal species, muscles, and behavior.' Another notes 'the main significance of this manuscript is the application of this new technology to different muscles and animal species during naturalistic behaviors.' The diversity of demonstrations across species and muscle types is treated as a major strength.

results.result: Myomatrix arrays were fabricated using polyimide and gold layers on a carrier wafer, with 20-40 μm thickness, PEDOT:PSS coating on electrode contacts reducing impedance to ≤5 kΩ, and a fabrication pipeline allowing rapid development of multiple designs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the fabrication methods without critique. One reviewer notes 'clear presentation of specifics of the fabrication and implantation, recording methods used, and data analysis' as a strength. Another states 'while technical details on the arrays have been published previously,' acknowledging prior validation of the fabrication approach. The methods are treated as adequately described and validated.

results.result: Motor unit waveforms were identified using adapted Kilosort 2.5 spike-sorting methods (band-passed 350-7000 Hz). The close electrode spacing in Myomatrix arrays results in sparser recordings better suited to Kilosort than traditional source-separation methods used for skin-surface EMG.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the analytical approach as appropriate. One reviewer specifically praises 'clear presentation of specifics of the fabrication and implantation, recording methods used, and data analysis.' The adaptation of neural spike-sorting methods to EMG data is implicitly endorsed through reviewers' acceptance of the isolated motor unit results without questioning the analysis methodology.

results.result: In over 100 Myomatrix injections in rhesus macaques, zero arrays broke leaving electrode material in muscle, representing substantial improvement over fine-wire approaches where wire tip breakage regularly occurs. Injectable Myomatrix devices appeared comparable or superior to fine-wire electrodes in ease of use and animal comfort.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the safety and usability claims without challenge. One reviewer notes 'the design included suture holes and pull-on tabs that facilitate implantation' as a strength. The zero-breakage rate in 100+ primate injections and favorable comparison to fine-wire methods are treated as credible evidence of improved safety and usability.

results.result: The songbird dataset included single-unit data from 8101 respiratory cycles collected over 74 minutes, with recordings ended by the experimenter rather than signal loss.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as part of the demonstrated recording stability across species. The songbird data is included in reviewers' praise for 'convincing examples of EMG recordings with high signal quality using this new technology from a wide array of animal species, muscles, and behavior.' The extended recording duration is consistent with the accepted claims about recording stability.

results.result: Future applications of Myomatrix technology could include human clinical diagnostics, reduced risk/discomfort in clinical EMG, combining with muscle force measurements, and integration with brain recordings to reveal how neural circuits shape motor neuron activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these forward-looking claims as reasonable implications. The editor states 'this new muscle recording method has the potential to provide new insight into a wide range of questions in motor neuroscience,' endorsing the broad potential applications. Reviewers note the manuscript 'will be of significant interest to researchers in motor systems and muscle physiology,' implicitly accepting the proposed future directions as valuable.

results.result: The expansion of access to high-resolution EMG signals across muscle groups, species, and behaviors is the chief impact of the Myomatrix project.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorse this summary of impact. One reviewer states 'the main significance of this manuscript is the application of this new technology to different muscles and animal species during naturalistic behaviors.' The editor calls it an 'important paper' with 'major technical advances' that 'has the potential to provide new insight into a wide range of questions in motor neuroscience,' fully supporting the claimed broad impact.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the core technical achievement (C1, C2) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval focuses on detailed fabrication specifications (C7-C10, C27-C28, C69-C74), while peer review emphasizes the broader significance of multi-species demonstrations. Both affirm the fundamental technical advance.

Partial overlap on fabrication claims (C7-C10, C27-C28). OpenEval provides detailed technical validation of specifications, while peer review accepts fabrication methods without critique, noting clear presentation of technical details and prior validation.

Both evaluate superior performance over traditional methods (C11-C14) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes statistical validation and appropriate methodology, while peer review highlights that claims are justified by data and signal quality is convincing.

Partial overlap on channel count advantage (C15-C16). OpenEval treats this as fundamental hardware difference with experimental demonstration, while peer review accepts multi-channel capability as part of demonstrated technical advantages.

Both evaluate chronic recording capability (C17-C21) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes C21 about behavioral limitation cannot be definitively proven, while peer review emphasizes recording stability as a key strength without qualification.

Both address songbird recording duration (C53). OpenEval provides specific quantitative measurements, while peer review accepts this as part of demonstrated recording stability across species without separate evaluation.

Perfect overlap on movement artifact claims (C22-C23), both SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes assessment relies on qualitative observation rather than systematic quantification, while peer review accepts absence of artifacts as demonstrated during naturalistic behaviors.

Both evaluate primate performance (C24-C26) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes within-animal comparison occurred in separate sessions, while peer review emphasizes this as part of compelling multi-species demonstration without methodological critique.

Both address safety and usability (C50-C52) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes C52's claim of 'comparable or superior' ease is qualitative without systematic measurement, while peer review accepts these claims without challenge.

Perfect overlap on breadth of applications (C29-C39), both SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes sample sizes per condition not specified, while peer review strongly endorses diversity of demonstrations as a major strength and key contribution.

Both evaluate analytical methods (C42-C49) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes no systematic validation of sorting accuracy provided, while peer review praises clear presentation and implicitly endorses spike-sorting adaptation through acceptance of results.

Both evaluate limitations of existing methods (C3-C5, C60-C62) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval characterizes these as motivation rather than new findings, while peer review accepts these claims as providing context for the significance of new technology.

Perfect overlap on future applications (C54-C55, C66-C67). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN because claims are explicitly speculative about future work, while peer review rates SUPPORTED, accepting them as reasonable implications with potential value.

Perfect overlap on significance summary (C68), both SUPPORTED. OpenEval bases assessment on breadth of demonstrations, while peer review explicitly endorses this as capturing the main significance and broad impact of the work.

OpenEval evaluates surgical methodology claims (C75-C80, C84-C85) as SUPPORTED, noting these are standard techniques adapted for specific hardware. No corresponding separate peer review evaluation found; likely subsumed in general methods acceptance.

OpenEval evaluates contextual citations (C40-C41) as SUPPORTED but notes these are factual statements from prior literature, not original findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
